opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things I find most interesting about the BFF experiments. Just to set the scene: you start with a soup of tapes filled with random bytes. You repeatedly pick two at random, stick them together, run the result as code in this minimal Brainfuck-like language, and pull them apart again. Initially almost nothing happens. Then, quite suddenly, you get a transition where self-replicating programs appear and take over the soup.

When you look at what those replicators are, they're not some single canonical "optimal replicator" that any run would converge on. Every run produces something different. The particular instructions, where the loops sit, which bytes are doing the copying and which are along for the ride: all of that is contingent. It depends on the specific history of who got concatenated with whom and what happened to be lying around. So a lot of the information in those genomes is frozen accident, in Crick's sense. It's there not because it's optimal but because it was there first and everything downstream came to depend on it.

What makes this more than "evolution has historical baggage" is the mechanism. The dynamics look much less like gradual point mutation and selection, and much more like symbiogenesis. Small fragments that can do something, maybe partially copy themselves or partially copy something else, get stuck together through these random interactions. Sometimes the combination does something neither part could do alone, and that composite becomes a new, more capable unit. So complexity grows by merger. The information in the genome is to a large degree a record of which earlier entities fused and in what order, a kind of nested historical record.

That changes how I think about information content. If you measured the tapes with something like compressibility, you'd see the shift from high-entropy noise to structured, repeated, compressible code. But the specific structure isn't determined by the physics of the system. The rules only define a space of possible replicators. Which one you get, and what gets incorporated along the way, is history. Function is real and selected for, but the encoding of that function is deeply path-dependent.

I think that's a general lesson about life, and probably about intelligence too. We tend to imagine biology as optimized design, but it's better understood as layer upon layer of contingent cooperative mergers that became locked in because they worked well enough together. Mitochondria are the classic example, but I think it goes all the way down, and BFF lets you watch it happen in a few minutes on a laptop with nothing put in by hand. Nobody designed a replicator. The combinatorics of things bumping into each other, plus the fact that whatever persists gets to keep interacting, is enough to generate it. And the particular replicator carries the fingerprints of its own improbable history.

r001.rationale: The response says partially copying fragments can combine into a composite that does what neither could alone and becomes a more capable unit, communicating a group advantage in replication.

r002.rationale: It describes genome information as a record of which earlier entities fused and in what order, and calls the encoding deeply path-dependent.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I love, because I think it gets at what information actually is in a living system, as opposed to what it is in a textbook.

So in BFF, you've got this soup of random tapes, each one just 64 bytes, and they interact by getting concatenated and run through a Brainfuck interpreter. Initially, the entropy is at maximum. There's no information in there in any meaningful sense. It's noise. And then at some point you get this phase transition, and suddenly the entropy drops, and you've got replicators, and the soup is full of structure.

Now, the naive way to think about the information that appears is to say, well, there's a program there now, it does replication, and the information is the specification of that function. But that's not really what's happening. What you actually see when you look at the genomes is that they're full of stuff that doesn't make sense in isolation. There's a byte here that only works because of a byte over there. There's a jump instruction whose target only exists because of some accident of what got copied in three thousand epochs ago. You can't look at any single position and say "this encodes X." The meaning of every piece is contingent on every other piece and on the history that produced it.

And that's exactly what Shannon information was always about, if you read him carefully. Information isn't a property of a symbol. It's a property of the relationship between a symbol and its context, between sender and receiver. In BFF, the "receiver" is the rest of the genome plus the interpreter plus the other tapes it's going to bump into. So when a replicator evolves a quirk that happens to exploit the way the head pointer wraps around, that quirk is only information relative to that whole ecology. Transplant it into a different soup and it's noise again.

I think this is why the genomes look so baroque when you actually read them. They don't look designed. They look like frozen accidents stacked on top of frozen accidents, where each accident became load-bearing because something downstream came to depend on it. That's contingent combination. And it's not a bug in the process. It's the mechanism. Complexity accretes precisely because the system can only build with what happens to already be there.

What I find really striking is how this reframes the question of where the information comes from. People sometimes ask, how can a random process generate information? And the answer is that the process isn't generating information in the sense of pulling bits from nowhere. It's doing selection on combinations. The space of possible 64-byte tapes is enormous, and almost all of it is dead. The replicators that persist are the ones whose particular contingent arrangement of bytes happens to be self-consistent under the dynamics. Over time those arrangements get more elaborate, they start to depend on each other, you get symbiosis between tapes, you get parasitism, and the information content is really just a record of which contingencies turned out to be compatible with each other.

That's very much how I think about biological genomes too. Most of what's in a genome isn't an instruction, it's a constraint that only makes sense given all the other constraints. So BFF, for me, is a way of watching that process happen from scratch, in a system simple enough that you can actually read the tape.

r001.rationale: The response describes mutually dependent bytes, symbiosis, and parasitism, but does not state that BFF instructions replicate more successfully together as a group than individually.

r002.rationale: The response calls the information a record of compatible contingencies and describes accumulated accidents, but does not clearly identify it as the history of contingent mergers that produced the final genome.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the information isn’t a property of a sequence in isolation. It’s a property of that sequence in relation to the environment it encounters—and in BFF, that environment includes the other sequences. What a particular piece of code does depends on what it interacts with.

So these contingent combinations are actually central. Two pieces can come together and produce a behavior that neither produces on its own. If that interaction helps them persist or replicate, then evolution can preserve it. Something that began as an accident becomes part of the structure on which subsequent evolution builds.

That means the genomes encode a kind of historical information: the consequences of encounters that happened to occur and combinations that happened to work. But you have to be careful about imagining each genome as a self-contained description of an organism. Some of the information is in the relationships. To understand what has evolved, you need to look at the interacting system, not just read off individual sequences.

r001.rationale: The response says interacting pieces can produce behaviors neither produces alone and that this may help them persist or replicate, but it does not clearly state that instructions replicate more successfully together as a group than individually.

r002.rationale: It describes genomes as encoding historical information from contingent encounters and combinations that worked, matching the history of mergers that produced the genome.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the information is relational. A piece of code doesn’t have some fixed fitness or meaning in isolation. What it does depends on the rest of the program, the other programs it encounters, and the history that brought those things together.

In BFF, programs interact and modify one another, so a combination that happens to arise can create the conditions for something to reproduce. Once that happens, selection can preserve that combination. What began as an accident becomes part of the machinery on which subsequent evolution depends.

So the genome is, in a sense, a record of contingencies that have become consequential. And you can’t necessarily understand that record by looking at individual instructions. You have to look at how they work together and at the ecology in which they’re operating.

r001.rationale: The response says a combination can enable reproduction, but does not clearly compare its replication success as a group with the instructions’ success individually.

r002.rationale: It describes the genome as a record of consequential contingencies and says the history of things coming together shaped it, communicating that the genome encodes the history of contingent combinations that produced it.
